reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Means and methods are the contractor's responsibility; final choice of drilling rigs and tools is made by the contractor based on: subsurface conditions presented in contract documents; site visit observations; contractor's personal experience in similar geology; available equipment; and documented experience from previous local projects. Choice of rigs and tools is critical to project success — minor changes in drilling tool can dramatically change excavation rate. Engineers and inspectors must understand general types of rigs and tools available in the US. Contractor normally provides rig/tool details in the drilled shaft installation plan.
key_points: Contractor responsible for means and methods; tool selection is contractor's risk
Engineers and inspectors must understand rig/tool types to develop appropriate specifications
Contractor provides rig/tool details in the drilled shaft installation plan
Pre-bid exploratory shaft excavation may be warranted to help bidders observe conditions
sections.applicability: All drilled shaft projects; specification development and inspection

sections.title: Drilling Machines
sections.body: Most US drilled shaft excavations use rotary drilling machines. Rig capacity measured by maximum torque and crowd (downward force). Force transmitted through kelly bar (round or square, single-piece up to ~60 ft or telescoping). In some rigs, kelly/tool dead weight provides crowd; others use hydraulic/mechanical devices for additional downward force. Mechanical drive systems: simple mechanical drive shaft or right angle drive from multi-speed transmission; lightweight; direct drive; limited capability to reach over tall casing. Hydraulic systems: higher torque range; moveable rotary travels up and down mast providing versatility for casing installation; typically heavier and more expensive. Machine mounting types: truck-mounted (most mobile; mast folds for road travel; mechanically driven with fixed rotary; limited capacity for rebar cage/casing handling); crane-mounted (substantial capabilities for bridge and marine work; dead weight drill collars or doughnuts provide crowd; rotary can be positioned 75+ ft from crane boom base; highly versatile with secondary lift line); crawler-mounted (less mobile than truck, excellent on-site mobility; most common for hydraulic rigs; lightweight versions for difficult access — slope stabilization, sound walls); excavator-mounted (hydraulic; advantage for restricted access and low headroom — under bridges, near utilities; limitations on depth and hole size); oscillator/rotator (hydraulic tool for advancing/extracting segmental casing; oscillator twists back-and-forth; rotator achieves full 360° rotation; enormous twisting forces require reaction system).
key_points: Rig capacity: maximum torque and crowd (downward force) through kelly bar
Hydraulic systems: higher torque, movable rotary — more versatile for casing operations
Truck-mounted: most mobile, limited for casing/cage handling, mechanically driven
Crane-mounted: best for marine/bridge, dead weight provides crowd, high versatility
Crawler-mounted: most common for hydraulic rigs, excellent on-site mobility
Oscillator: back-and-forth rotation; Rotator: full 360° — for segmental casing installation

sections.title: Tools for Excavation
sections.body: Rotary tools: (1) Continuous-flight auger — spiral flighting around a central shaft; used for dry, cohesive soils; standard auger with a fishtail or pilot bit for soft soils, stepped auger with carbide teeth for hard soils; flight lifts cuttings to surface; diameter 12-84 in.; (2) Bucket auger — cylindrical bucket with cutting teeth at the bottom; cuttings collected inside bucket; used for soft to medium soils; especially effective in sandy soils below water table; (3) Core barrel — hollow cylinder with cutting teeth at the bottom; used for rock coring; (4) Full-face roller-bit (tricone) — used for hard rock penetration by percussive/rotary combination; requires circulation for cuttings removal; (5) Single-pass full-face bit — fixed cutter bit; used for cutting through rock. Rock tools: step-taper reamers, full-face bits with button bits or drag bits. Percussion and other tools: (1) Air/hydraulic hammer (DTH) — down-the-hole hammer with drill bit mounted at the bottom; operates by percussion; effective for hard rock; requires air circulation for cuttings removal; (2) Clamshell bucket — two hinged jaws; used in very soft or flowing soils and in the wet method; limited penetration into hard soils; (3) Eccentric underreamer — used to form belled or underreamed base to increase bearing area.
key_points: Continuous-flight auger: dry cohesive soils; lifts cuttings to surface
Bucket auger: collects cuttings inside; effective in sandy soils below water table
Core barrel: rock coring with hollow cylinder and cutting teeth
Roller-bit / tricone: hard rock; requires fluid circulation for cuttings removal
DTH hammer: percussion + rotation for hard rock; requires air circulation
Clamshell: very soft or flowing soils; wet construction
Underreamer: forms bell at base to increase bearing area
sections.applicability: Tool selection based on soil/rock type and groundwater conditions

sections.title: Other Techniques
sections.body: Base cleanout tools for wet holes: airlifts (pneumatic pumping), submersible pumps with cleanout shovels, cleaning buckets, and pump/vacuum systems remove loose cuttings from base of wet excavation. Aggressive use of cleanout tools in cohesionless sands can advance the shaft excavation — use downhole camera to evaluate effectiveness. Stabilizing soils: on rare occasions permeation or compaction grouting may stabilize particularly unstable strata or reduce water inflow. Baker et al. (1982) demonstrated pre-excavation grouting to reduce inflow and permit under-ream construction in granular soils (Chicago examples). Base grouting through sleeve-port tubes described in Chapter 3 and Appendix H.
key_points: Airlifts, submersible pumps, cleaning buckets used for base cleanout in wet holes
Aggressive cleanout tool use in sands can over-excavate — verify with downhole camera
Pre-excavation grouting can stabilize unstable strata and reduce water inflow
Base grouting improves base resistance in granular soils
sections.applicability: Wet construction base cleanout; challenging soil conditions

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: Chapter described drilling machines and tools for drilled shaft construction. Choice of tools and equipment is generally the contractor's responsibility. Engineers must be knowledgeable of drilling equipment to provide appropriate specifications, constructable and cost-efficient designs, and sufficient subsurface information for bidders. Tools and equipment planned by contractor should be described in the drilled shaft installation plan and documented in construction records.
key_points: Contractor's drilled shaft installation plan must describe planned tools and equipment
Engineers must understand equipment to write appropriate specifications
Sufficient subsurface information required for bidders to make informed equipment decisions
